questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the pest to natural enemy ratio in a field
questions.stem: Cartographic annotation 4401 gives a pest population of 2400 per hectare with a natural enemy population of 600 per hectare; what is the ratio of pests to natural enemies?
questions.explanation: Divide the pest count by the natural enemy count: 2400 divided by 600 gives 4, so there are four pests for every natural enemy. Ratios like this help judge whether biological control is holding.
questions.hint: Divide the pest count by the predator count.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a shared resource is overused by its users
questions.stem: Common-pool note 4402 asks for an explanation of why a shared grazing resource is overused even when every user knows it is finite.

answer.exemplar: Each grazier takes the private benefit of adding one more animal, which is the extra weight gained on their own herd, while the cost of the extra animal is spread across the whole commons as thinner pasture for everyone. When the number of users is large and each user has only a small share of the resource, the individual gain from extra use is larger than the individual share of the damage, so each user is rewarded for taking more than the sustainable share. The result is that the aggregate of individually rational choices destroys the resource that all of them depend on, and only a binding agreement, an enforced quota or a change in the reward structure can reverse it.

questions.explanation: Each user gains privately while the damage is shared, so individual rationality produces collective overuse. The item tests the incentive structure rather than any claim about user ignorance.
questions.hint: Think about who gains and who pays.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Select the practice that reduces fertiliser losses to water
questions.stem: Legend entry 4403 asks which agricultural practice most directly reduces fertiliser losses to nearby watercourses.

options.text: Applying fertiliser when the soil is already wet, so it dissolves into the soil water
options.misconception: thinks wet soil protects nutrients from runoff

options.text: Applying fertiliser at the crop's real need and avoiding application before heavy rain
Spreading fertiliser on the headland, where the slope is least and runoff is least
options.misconception: moves the loss to another part of the same field

options.text: Using a higher rate per hectare so that fewer applications are needed each season
options.misconception: assumes fewer applications means less total nutrient

questions.explanation: Matching the rate to crop need and avoiding application before heavy rain keeps nutrients in the root zone. Wet or sloping ground raises losses, and headlands only relocate them.
questions.hint: Think about when nutrients can move.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a closed loop on a materials flow map

stimulus.body: A cartographer's note records that a municipal survey found that a large share of the tonnage of materials entering the city left as mixed waste within a year, while a smaller share of the same materials was collected separately and processed. The note asks that the material flows on the plan be drawn so that the returning share is shown as a loop rather than a line off the edge.

questions.stem: Projection note 4404 asks which change the revised map of material flows is intended to represent.

options.text: A reduction in the total amount of material consumed within the city boundary
options.misconception: reads the loop as reduced total consumption

options.text: A shift from landfill disposal to exporting the same waste abroad
options.misconception: mistakes redirection for an export of material

options.text: An increase in the share of materials that is collected and treated as waste
options.misconception: confuses better collection with material reuse

options.text: A larger share of materials kept in use instead of becoming waste

questions.explanation: A loop on the plan means material is recovered and used again rather than becoming waste, the defining idea of a circular economy. The note does not describe reduced consumption or exporting waste.
questions.hint: Ask what the returning loop represents.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Calculate an ecological deficit from footprint and capacity
questions.stem: Sheet calculation 4405 gives a household ecological footprint of 3.6 global hectares against a biocapacity of 2.4 global hectares; what is the ecological deficit in global hectares?
questions.explanation: Subtract biocapacity from the footprint: 3.6 minus 2.4 gives a deficit of 1.2 global hectares. The deficit is the extra productive land needed beyond the household's own share of it.
questions.hint: Subtract the capacity from the demand.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain the weakness of allocating from historical abstraction
questions.stem: Licence note 4406 asks for an explanation of why a water allocation licence based only on a historical abstraction figure is difficult to defend.

answer.exemplar: A licence built on past abstraction assumes the past was a fair and repeatable basis for the future, and it rarely is. Abstraction depends on rainfall and river levels, so a figure taken from a wet decade or from a period of heavy industrial demand is higher than the average supply the river can carry in a dry one. As climate alters the pattern of rainfall and as demand grows, the licensed volume can exceed what is available, and the licence then guarantees an over-abstraction rather than a sustainable share. Allocation policy therefore increasingly works from the sustainable yield of the catchment, adjusted for ecological needs and for the reliability of the flow at the driest times rather than from a historical average.

questions.explanation: A historical figure may embed a wet period and past demand, so it can licence more than the river can reliably supply. The item tests why allocations are now based on sustainable yield.
questions.hint: Think about what a past average hides.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Identify a nonpoint source of water pollution
questions.stem: Catchment sheet 4407 asks which of the following is a nonpoint source of water pollution.

options.text: Nitrate washed from farm fields into ditches and streams after heavy rainfall
A discharge pipe from a factory emptying effluent into a river at one location
options.misconception: confuses a fixed outfall with a diffuse source

options.text: A leaking sewer pipe spilling sewage into a stream at one point
options.misconception: treats a single pipe failure as a diffuse source

options.text: A permitted outfall releasing treated effluent from a sewage works
options.misconception: ignores the point nature of a permitted discharge

questions.explanation: A nonpoint source is diffuse and travels with runoff, so field nitrate carried by rain is the clearest example. Pipes and outfalls deliver pollution at one place, which makes them point sources.
questions.hint: Ask whether the source is one place or many.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a digester is a branch in a process flow diagram

stimulus.body: A cartographer's note describes a treatment works drawn on a site plan. The influent enters a primary clarifier, then an aeration basin, then a secondary clarifier, then a filter, and finally a disinfection contact tank before the outfall. The note records that the sludge stream leaves the two clarifiers and goes to a separate digester tank before dewatering.

questions.stem: Site plan note 4408 asks why the note should show the sludge digester as a branch from the clarifiers rather than as a stage in the main line.

options.text: Because digestion is optional and the plant can run without a digester tank at all
options.misconception: treats sludge digestion as discretionary

options.text: Because the digester is only used when the plant handles industrial waste
options.misconception: invents a waste type that triggers digestion

options.text: Because the digester treats the solids stream while the liquid continues to the next stage
Because the digester is placed upstream of the aeration basin in the real works
options.misconception: moves the digester to a position the plan does not show

questions.explanation: A digester receives the settled solids from the clarifiers and treats them apart from the liquid, which continues to the outfall. The digester is an essential part of the works, not an optional extra.
questions.hint: Follow the two separate streams.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the percentage reduction in a pest population
questions.stem: Field annotation 4409 gives a pest population of 1500 per hectare before treatment and 300 per hectare after treatment; what is the percentage reduction achieved?
questions.explanation: The fall is 1200 per hectare, and 1200 divided by the original 1500 gives 0.80, which is 80 per cent. Reporting the reduction against the starting density allows fields to be compared.
questions.hint: Divide the fall by the starting population.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain the mechanisms that save a shared resource
questions.stem: Commons note 4410 asks for an explanation of how a shared resource can be saved when it is clear that voluntary restraint will not happen.

answer.exemplar: Voluntary restraint fails in a commons because each user is rewarded immediately for taking more, and the collective loss appears only later and is spread thinly. Three mechanisms can change that. Rules backed by monitoring and enforcement set a clear limit that no single user can gain from breaking. Quotas or permits divide the resource into shares, so each user knows exactly what is theirs and gains nothing by taking more. Assigning the resource to a single owner with an interest in its long term condition removes the collective action problem entirely, because the owner now receives the whole benefit of restraint. In practice these are often combined with the payment of the costs of monitoring.

questions.explanation: Enforcement, quotas and ownership change the incentive so that restraint becomes individually rational. The item tests the mechanisms that resolve collective action, not merely the diagnosis.
questions.hint: Think about changing what one user gains.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect of applying fertiliser beyond crop demand
questions.stem: Water quality map 4411 asks what happens when the amount of fertiliser applied to a field exceeds what the crop can take up.

options.text: The surplus nitrogen and phosphorus build up and move toward watercourses
The surplus is stored harmlessly in the soil until the next season of crop growth
options.misconception: assumes all surplus nutrient is safely retained

options.text: The crop absorbs the extra nutrients and produces correspondingly more biomass
options.misconception: assumes plants take up fertiliser without limit

options.text: The surplus nitrogen is released as nitrogen gas and leaves the soil harmlessly
options.misconception: treats denitrification as a harmless loss of surplus

questions.explanation: Surplus nutrient accumulates, so nitrate leaches and phosphorus washes into surface water, and both contribute to eutrophication. Plants cannot take unlimited nutrient, and gaseous losses are small.
questions.hint: Think about where the surplus ends up.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Identify the design features that make reuse possible

stimulus.body: A cartographer's note describes a refurbishment scheme in which old door panels are removed from a public building, cleaned and re-used in refurbished buildings nearby, while the removed fittings that cannot be re-used are separated by material and sent for recycling. The note records that the design of the new fittings was chosen so they could be removed without damaging the panels.

questions.stem: Scheme note 4412 asks which two design features the scheme relies on most.

options.text: Reducing the number of materials used and reducing the mass of the new fittings
options.misconception: mistakes efficiency measures for the design of reuse

options.text: Extending the life of the building and reducing the cost of the new fittings
options.misconception: treats cost and service life as the operative features

options.text: Recycling the fittings and disposing of the old panels at the end of the scheme
options.misconception: claims the panels are discarded rather than reused

options.text: Designing for disassembly and arranging for components to be returned and reused

questions.explanation: The scheme works because components come apart without damage and are then returned for reuse, which is what a circular design requires. Efficiency gains help but do not close the loop, and the panels are reused.
questions.hint: Ask what makes the loop physically possible.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the carbon share of an ecological footprint
questions.stem: Carbon share 4413 gives a country's ecological footprint as 4.8 million global hectares of carbon uptake demand and 2.2 million global hectares of demand for food and fibre; what is the carbon share of the total footprint as a percentage?
questions.explanation: The total is 4.8 plus 2.2, or 7.0 million global hectares, and 4.8 divided by 7.0 gives about 0.686, roughly 68.6 per cent. The share shows how dominant carbon demand is in this accounting.
questions.hint: Add the components, then take the share.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain the purpose of an ecological flow reserve
questions.stem: Ecological flow note 4414 asks for an explanation of why an ecological flow reserve is written into a water allocation scheme.

answer.exemplar: An allocation scheme that divides the whole flow between abstractors can, in a dry year, leave a river with so little water that its temperature rises, its dissolved oxygen falls and its channel dries into disconnected pools. These changes kill fish, push riverine species out and remove the habitat that the surrounding landscape depends on. An ecological flow reserve sets aside the quantity of water that must remain in the channel for the system to function, and it is taken before abstractors are served. Giving it legal priority means the reserve is protected in the years when it matters most, rather than left to whatever water happens to be left over after every other claim has been met.

questions.explanation: An ecological reserve guarantees the flow a river needs to function, and giving it priority means it survives dry years. The item tests why the reserve is set aside before other claims are met.
questions.hint: Think about who is served first in a dry year.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why diffuse pollution is harder to control
questions.stem: Catchment map note 4415 asks why controlling nonpoint pollution is generally harder than controlling a single point source.

options.text: Because nonpoint sources always carry more pollutants than point sources do
options.misconception: compares the sources by load rather than by difficulty of control

options.text: Because nonpoint sources are always located in the centre of the catchment
options.misconception: invents a location rule for diffuse sources

options.text: Because the sources are spread across the land and are carried by runoff
Because point sources are already fully controlled by modern treatment works
options.misconception: assumes point sources need no further control

questions.explanation: Diffuse sources arise from many activities spread over the catchment and reach water through runoff, so there is no single outlet to treat. A point source has a defined location that can be permitted and enforced.
questions.hint: Think about whether there is one outlet.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Identify the first stage of a drinking water treatment train

stimulus.body: A cartographer's note describes a drinking water works drawn on a site plan. Raw water is drawn from a reservoir, screened, mixed with a coagulant in a mixing chamber, allowed to settle in a basin, filtered through sand beds, aerated, and finally dosed with chlorine in a contact tank before distribution. The note records that the engineer asked for the aeration step to be moved to the start of the train to save pipework.

questions.stem: Process flow note 4416 asks which stage normally comes first in a drinking water treatment sequence.

options.text: Disinfection, so that any incoming pathogens are killed before other treatment
options.misconception: puts the sterilisation step at the start of the sequence

options.text: Coagulation and sedimentation, to remove the suspended material that clouds the water
Activated carbon filtration, to strip the unpleasant tastes from the raw water
options.misconception: treats taste removal as the primary treatment step

options.text: Membrane filtration, because all the later stages depend on membrane quality
options.misconception: assumes membranes are always the first treatment step

questions.explanation: Coagulation and sedimentation come first because they remove the suspended solids that would otherwise foul later filters and shield microbes from disinfection. Carbon and membranes address specific contaminants later.
questions.hint: Think about which step protects the later ones.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Calculate pest density after a chemical control application
questions.stem: Field map note 4417 gives a pest population of 4800 per hectare, a natural enemy population of 900 per hectare and a chemical control that reduces the pest population by 40 per cent; what is the pest density per hectare after the treatment?
questions.explanation: A 40 per cent reduction leaves 60 per cent of the population: 4800 multiplied by 0.60 gives 2880 per hectare. The natural enemy count is useful for judging whether the reduction will hold.
questions.hint: Multiply the population by the fraction remaining.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a degraded common may fail to recover
questions.stem: Commons plate 4418 asks for an explanation of how a shared resource can collapse and then fail to recover even after use is reduced.

answer.exemplar: Once a shared resource has been overused, it can sit below the threshold at which it regenerates. A grazed pasture stripped of its seed bank and its deep-rooted plants becomes bare, and bare ground invites further erosion and shrub encroachment, so the land that would have reseeded quickly now seeds poorly. Reduced grazing alone does not reverse this, because the ecological state has shifted and the recovery path is longer and slower than the original degradation. Management therefore has to go beyond simply taking fewer animals and has to rebuild the plant community, control invading shrubs and reduce erosion while the stocking pressure is kept low, or the resource remains trapped in the degraded state.

questions.explanation: Overuse can push a resource past a threshold where it cannot regenerate, so reduced use alone does not restore it. The item tests the idea of an alternative stable state.
questions.hint: Think about the state of the resource itself.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Select the measure that reduces phosphorus loss from grazed land
questions.stem: Nutrient map note 4419 asks which practice most reliably reduces the phosphorus lost to a watercourse from a grazed field.

options.text: Increasing the rate of nitrogen fertiliser so that grass grows faster and covers more soil
options.misconception: treats nitrogen application as the route to phosphorus control

options.text: Cutting drainage ditches deeper so that surface water leaves the field quickly
options.misconception: speeds the delivery of phosphorus to the watercourse

options.text: Maintaining good ground cover with clover and rye so phosphorus is held in the soil
Spreading slurry in early spring when the ground is soft and the rain is light
options.misconception: confuses soft ground with a low risk of runoff

questions.explanation: Phosphorus is held on soil particles and organic matter, so continuous cover keeps it in the root zone and reduces particulate lost in runoff. More nitrogen and faster drainage lose phosphorus to water.
questions.hint: Think about what holds phosphorus in place.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Select the indicator that distinguishes genuine circularity

stimulus.body: A cartographer's note describes a comparison drawn between two production systems. In the first, the same service is delivered with 4 units of new material per unit of output, with almost nothing recovered at the end of life. In the second the same service is delivered with 1.5 units of new material per unit of output, because most of the components are reused and the rest are recycled. The note records that the second system also handles a greater total tonnage of material each year, because the products last longer and are serviced more often.

questions.stem: Circularity note 4420 asks which indicator best distinguishes genuine circularity from simply burning more fossil fuel.

options.text: A smaller quantity of virgin material input per unit of service delivered
A larger total tonnage of materials handled within the economy each year
options.misconception: mistakes throughput for circularity

options.text: A higher proportion of material collected and sorted at the end of life
options.misconception: counts recycling alone as circularity

options.text: A shorter average time between manufacturing a product and selling it
options.misconception: uses a distribution speed metric as a circularity measure

questions.explanation: Circularity means meeting the same need with less new material, so input per unit of service is the telling measure. Handling more tonnage or collecting more waste says nothing about keeping material in use.
questions.hint: Ask what replaces the need for new material.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the total footprint of a population
questions.stem: Population sheet 4421 gives a population of 2500000 with a per person ecological footprint of 2.5 global hectares and a total biocapacity of 5.0 million global hectares; what is the ecological footprint of the whole population in millions of global hectares?
questions.explanation: Multiply the population by the per person footprint: 2500000 times 2.5 gives 6250000 global hectares, or 6.25 million. Against the 5.0 million available, that leaves a deficit of 1.25 million.
questions.hint: Multiply people by footprint each.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why tradable permits differ from fixed quotas
questions.stem: Permit note 4422 asks for an explanation of why water allocation schemes increasingly use tradable permits rather than fixed quotas.

answer.exemplar: A fixed quota gives each abstractor a volume and leaves it with no incentive to use it efficiently, because a unit saved on one farm is simply a unit lost to that farm, while the river keeps running at full abstraction. A tradable permit separates the right to take water from the act of taking it. Abstractors who can meet their need cheaply by conserving or by re-using water can sell permits to those whose need is expensive to satisfy, so the total abstraction stays within the cap while the water goes where it is worth most. The scheme also makes the value of conservation visible in money, which a quota never does, and the regulator keeps control by issuing the permits and setting the cap on how many are outstanding.

questions.explanation: Trading lets water go to its highest value use while total withdrawal stays capped, which fixed quotas do not do. The item tests the incentive difference between the two schemes.
questions.hint: Think about who can buy and sell the right to abstract.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Select the most effective control on diffuse agricultural pollution
questions.stem: Buffer note 4423 asks which measure is the most effective way of reducing diffuse agricultural pollution entering a stream.

options.text: Constructing a large treatment plant at the point where the river leaves the area
options.misconception: assumes a single plant can treat diffuse pollution

options.text: Restoring buffer strips of permanent vegetation along the stream and field edges
Installing a regulator at the abstraction offtake to stop pollutants entering the channel
options.misconception: assumes pollutants can be filtered out of the channel water

options.text: Requiring farms to report their fertiliser use each year to the regulator
options.misconception: treats reporting as a direct reduction measure

questions.explanation: Permanent vegetation at the field and stream edge intercepts runoff, traps sediment and takes up nutrients before they reach the channel, so it acts where pollution is generated. A downstream plant cannot remove dissolved nutrients.
questions.hint: Act close to where the pollution starts.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain the function of preliminary treatment works

stimulus.body: A cartographer's note records a treatment works whose plan shows an inlet screen, a grit chamber, an aeration basin, a clarifier and a filter in series. The note records that the inlet screen and grit chamber are described as preliminary works, and that the engineer argued that the design would be simpler and cheaper if the preliminary stages were left out because the incoming water was already clean.

questions.stem: Preliminary works note 4424 asks what the engineer's argument overlooks about the preliminary works.

options.text: That preliminary stages are always the most expensive part of any works
options.misconception: rejects the argument on cost grounds not in the note

options.text: That clean incoming water still carries grit, fibres and other floating material
options.misconception: assumes clean water carries no solids at all

options.text: That preliminary works can only be justified where the water is very dirty
options.misconception: suggests grit removal needs extreme pollution

options.text: That grit and debris reaching the aeration stage would damage and block the plant

questions.explanation: Preliminary works protect everything downstream, because grit and fibres reaching pumps and aeration equipment cause wear and blockages. Their value lies in preventing damage, which the simplicity argument overlooks.
questions.hint: Think about what reaches the aeration stage.

questions.explanation: Multiply the nightly catch by the number of nights: 12 times 3 gives 36 moths. Trap catches are used to set action thresholds rather than to spray automatically.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why common-pool resources sit between sectors
questions.stem: Governance note 4426 asks for an explanation of why common-pool resources are often the ones that users expect the government to look after.

answer.exemplar: A fishery, a grazing common or a shared irrigation canal is costly to manage as a private good, because the cost of monitoring and enforcing limits falls on one owner while the benefit of the intact resource is spread across many users. Conversely, if the resource is left to the market, each user will take more than the sustainable share, because the cost of the extra use is borne by everyone. This double bind, high private cost of stewardship combined with strong incentives to over-exploit, is why common-pool resources sit awkwardly in either the private or the purely administrative sector, and why they are typically run with community involvement and rules agreed and enforced locally.

questions.explanation: The cost of guarding a shared resource falls on one body while its benefits are spread, and markets push users to over-exploit. The item tests why such resources sit between private and state provision.
questions.hint: Think about who pays and who benefits.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Select the outcome that shows reduced fertiliser loading working
questions.stem: Lake map note 4427 asks which outcome best indicates that reducing fertiliser loading in a catchment is working.

options.text: The algal bloom in the lake appears earlier each spring than in previous years
options.misconception: reads an earlier bloom as improving water quality

options.text: The farmers in the catchment report higher yields from the same fertiliser inputs
options.misconception: mistakes farm productivity for lake condition

options.text: The summer algal bloom is smaller and the oxygen level stays higher in deeper water
The number of farms applying fertiliser in the catchment falls year on year
options.misconception: uses an activity count rather than a water quality measure

questions.explanation: Fertiliser drives algal growth, and when the bloom shrinks, less organic matter is decomposed and less oxygen consumed, so deeper water stays oxygenated. An earlier bloom or a falling farm count says little about the lake.
questions.hint: Look for a change in the lake itself.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a circular economy from a linear one

stimulus.body: A cartographer's note describes a production flow drawn as two diagrams. The first shows raw material entering a factory, a product leaving and a waste stream going to landfill, with no arrow returning. The second shows the same raw material entering, the product leaving, and a loop returning components to the start of the flow after use, with a smaller arrow to incineration. The note asks that the second diagram be labelled as the more circular of the two.

questions.stem: Circular map note 4428 asks which of the following best describes the difference between a circular economy and a linear one.

options.text: A circular economy keeps products in use and retains the value of their materials
A circular economy uses fewer materials but disposes of products in the same way
options.misconception: confuses reduced input with retained value

options.text: A circular economy increases total production while ignoring where materials go
options.misconception: treats higher output as the goal

options.text: A circular economy relies on incineration so that materials return as energy to the process
options.misconception: mistakes energy recovery for material circularity

questions.explanation: The circular approach keeps products circulating through use, repair and remanufacture, so material value is retained rather than lost at disposal. Using less material still discards products, and incineration destroys material.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to a product after its first use.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the ecological overshoot of a region
questions.stem: Overshoot sheet 4429 records that a region has a biocapacity of 8.4 million global hectares and a footprint of 10.5 million global hectares; what is the total ecological overshoot in millions of global hectares?
questions.explanation: Subtract the biocapacity from the footprint: 10.5 minus 8.4 gives an overshoot of 2.1 million global hectares. Overshoot measures demand placed on ecosystems beyond what the region can regenerate in a year.
questions.hint: Subtract the capacity from the footprint.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how drought restrictions are prioritised
questions.stem: Drought plan note 4430 asks for an explanation of how a drought plan decides which abstractors are cut off first.

answer.exemplar: A drought plan sets tiers of restriction that are triggered by the state of the resource rather than by a fixed calendar, so that the severity of the cut reflects how depleted the source actually is. Within the first tier, voluntary saving and publicity are used, because they are cheap and do not require enforcement. When restrictions become mandatory, abstractors are prioritised by criteria agreed in advance: critical public supply such as hospitals and drinking water comes first, then ecological and environmental needs, then licences with essential industrial and irrigation uses, and finally non-essential and speculative abstraction. Agreeing the hierarchy beforehand is what keeps the decisions fair and defensible when the pressure is highest and time is short.

questions.explanation: Ties restrictions to the state of the resource and agrees the priority order in advance, so decisions are consistent and defensible. The item tests how allocation is made under scarcity.
questions.hint: Think about order of priority and triggers.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why a hedgerow margin reduces pest damage
questions.stem: Margin note 4431 asks which feature of a hedgerow margin best explains the lower pest damage recorded there alongside a grass strip and a bare margin.

options.text: The hedge casts shade on the crop, so the shaded plants are less attacked
options.misconception: invents a shading effect as the mechanism

options.text: The hedge is closer to the field edge, so spray drift reaches it less often
options.misconception: links border position to pest damage

options.text: The hedge root system lifts moisture, so the crop near it suffers drought stress
options.misconception: suggests drought stress reduces pest damage

options.text: The hedge provides habitat for predators and parasitoids that attack the pests

questions.explanation: Hedgerows and margins provide refuge, alternative prey and nectar for natural enemies, so populations of predators and parasitoids build up and suppress the pest. Shade, spray drift and root competition do not explain a consistent difference in pest attack.
questions.hint: Think about what lives inside the hedge.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: State the essence of the tragedy of the commons

stimulus.body: A cartographer's note records a grazing common shared by several households, in which each family keeps its own herd of sheep. The note records that the note author asked for the map to carry a note explaining why the herds grew larger over ten years even though every family could see the grass thinning.

questions.stem: Commons definition 4432 asks which description best captures the essence of the tragedy of the commons.

options.text: A shared resource is exhausted because each user takes more than its fair share
options.misconception: blames greedy users instead of the incentive structure

options.text: Shared users with individual incentives act together to destroy a resource they all need
options.misconception: misses the link between individual incentives and collective loss

options.text: A government takes a resource into public ownership and manages it badly
options.misconception: reduces the idea to a failure of public management

options.text: A private company buys a shared resource and extracts it as quickly as possible
options.misconception: confuses the tragedy with ordinary commercial extraction

questions.explanation: The tragedy arises because individual incentives push each user to take more while the shared loss is spread, so collective action destroys the resource for everyone. It is about the incentive structure, not about who owns the resource.
questions.hint: Think about incentives, not ownership.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why repair is central to circular thinking
questions.stem: Repair note 4434 asks for an explanation of why repair is central to a circular economy rather than a side activity within it.

answer.exemplar: A product that can be repaired stays valuable because the work needed to keep it in use is far smaller than the work of making a new one, and the material, energy and capital already committed to that product are not wasted. Repair also creates a different supply chain, one based on skills, spare parts and local labour rather than on the extraction of new raw material. Where products are designed so that the worn component can be reached and replaced, the lifespan of the whole product lengthens and the waste stream shrinks. Where they are sealed or glued together, no repair is possible at all, so the design decision made years earlier determines how circular the system can be.

questions.explanation: Repair preserves the value already invested in a product and its materials, and it depends on design choices made at manufacture. The item tests why repair belongs at the centre of circular thinking.
questions.hint: Think about the value already sunk into a product.

options.misconception: mislabels the treatment level shown by the plan

options.text: A primary works, because the main treatment is the settling in the first tank

options.text: A secondary biological works with primary sedimentation and tertiary polishing
A septic tank arrangement, because the solids are pumped away to the digester
options.misconception: mistakes a digester for a septic tank

questions.explanation: The plan shows primary settlement, aeration and secondary settlement, making a secondary biological works, and filtration and disinfection add tertiary polishing. The aeration basin rules out a primary works.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Contrast an atmospheric commons with a depleted fishery
questions.stem: Atmosphere note 4438 asks for an explanation of how atmospheric pollution differs from a depleted fishery as a commons.

answer.exemplar: The atmosphere differs from a depleted fishery in ways that change the policy response. Its capacity to absorb a pollutant is large and no single emitter can see the harm it causes or the benefit of cutting back, and there is no clear point at which the resource is exhausted. Emissions from many sources mix in a single air mass, so a country or city cannot readily separate its own contribution from the air it receives from elsewhere. As a result the tools that work on a local common, monitoring and enforceable quotas tied to a visible stock, are much weaker, and the policy burden falls on international agreement about emissions rather than on a single authority.

questions.explanation: An atmospheric commons is large, invisible and mixed, so local monitoring and quotas are weak tools. The item tests how the nature of the shared resource shapes the governance response.
questions.hint: Think about whether anyone can see the stock or the harm.

questions.learningObjective: Identify a genuine closed material loop

stimulus.body: A cartographer's note describes a materials flow diagram for a town. options.text: Collecting used cooking oil and processing it into new fuel for vehicles

options.misconception: describes a linear design as circular

questions.explanation: Collecting and processing used cooking oil into fuel keeps the material in productive use through a real chain, which is what closing a loop means. Incineration destroys material and single-use packaging is the opposite.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain the limits of trading water licences
questions.stem: Transfer note 4442 asks for an explanation of why transferring a water licence between two users can be contentious even when the total abstracted stays the same.

answer.exemplar: An abstraction licence is a claim on a shared river, and a transfer changes who holds that claim without changing the volume drawn, so the river itself is no better or worse off. The transfer can nevertheless be unwelcome for reasons that are about position and history rather than hydrology. The receiving user may be drawing from a different reach, so the water removed is no longer taken from the same place, and downstream users and the ecological reserve can lose the flow they were relying on at that point. Local communities also see a licence as a connection to a place and a way of life. Without rules about which transfers are acceptable, a market that is neutral on the total can still be seen as unfair in its effect.

questions.explanation: A licence transfer can change where water is taken from and who bears the local effects, even if the total is unchanged. The item tests the limits of treating licences as simple tradable assets.
questions.hint: Think about location as well as volume.

Adding more tile drainage to fields so that surplus water leaves the soil quickly

options.misconception: counts a yield gain as a water quality gain

questions.explanation: Vegetated ditches and buffer strips intercept runoff, trap sediment-bound phosphorus and take up nutrients before they reach the lake. More tile drainage speeds delivery, and no application change creates a filter.
questions.hint: Think about intercepting the runoff.

options.text: A works that screens and digests solids and then treats the liquid biologically

questions.explanation: The plan separates solids handling from liquid treatment: solids are removed and digested, while the liquid goes through aeration, filtration and disinfection. That is a works with a dedicated solids stream, not an anaerobic scheme.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a price signal alone does not fix a commons
questions.stem: Pricing note 4446 asks for an explanation of why fixing a price on a shared resource does not by itself solve the tragedy of the commons.

answer.exemplar: A price can steer behaviour when the resource can be traded and the regulator can control the total, but a commons usually fails precisely because the total is not controlled and the users are numerous and dispersed. If each grazier is charged for each animal, the charge has to be set at a level that makes the marginal animal unattractive to everyone, which is costly to monitor and often prohibitive for small users. If the charge is set lower to keep it affordable, the total number of animals still rises and the resource still degrades, because the aggregate demand is what matters. Prices work where the quantity is capped and tradable; where neither holds, allocation rules and monitoring capacity matter more than the price signal.

questions.explanation: A price only steers users where the total use is capped and monitored, and a commons usually lacks both. The item tests why pricing alone leaves the collective problem unsolved.
questions.hint: Think about whether the total use is controlled.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the delay between a fertiliser change and a river response
questions.stem: Lag note 4447 asks how a delay between a fertiliser change and a river response is explained when the underlying aquifer is deep, unconfined and slow draining with a partial clay seal.

options.text: The delay is caused by the time needed for farmers to change how they plough the soil
options.misconception: attributes the lag to a farm practice not in the note

options.text: The delay is caused by the monitoring station taking longer to detect a rising trend
options.misconception: suggests an instrument or reporting delay

options.text: The delay is caused by nitrate being converted into other nitrogen compounds in the soil
options.misconception: invents a transformation not mentioned in the note

options.text: The delay is caused by water and nitrate stored in the aquifer taking time to reach the river

questions.explanation: Nitrate applied at the surface does not reach the river immediately, because it must percolate, be stored in the aquifer and travel through groundwater to the river. A deep, slow aquifer with a partial seal lags the change by years.
questions.hint: Think about the pathway from soil to river.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why irrigation allocations are expressed per hectare
questions.stem: Irrigation note 4450 asks for an explanation of why irrigation allocations are often tied to area of land rather than to volume of water.

answer.exemplar: An allocation expressed in millimetres of depth over a hectare has a practical meaning that an allocation in cubic metres does not. It tells the farmer directly how much the crop can be given, it can be checked against the crop's requirement for the season and the soil's storage capacity, and it makes the allocation portable between fields of different sizes, so that a farmer who leases more land does not automatically gain more water. It also allows the regulator to compare areas planted under different crops with very different water needs. The weakness of the approach is that it assumes uniform application, so it under-rewards the farmers who can achieve the same yield with less water and it can encourage cropping in places where water should not be applied at all.

questions.explanation: A depth-based allocation matches the crop's need and travels with the area rather than with the landholder. The item tests the reasoning behind expressing allocations per hectare.
questions.hint: Think about what the farmer needs to know.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how users can manage a shared resource themselves
questions.stem: Community note 4454 asks for an explanation of how shared grazing land can be managed successfully by the users themselves.

answer.exemplar: Communities that have managed grazing commons for generations do so through rules that are detailed, locally specific and enforced by the people who depend on the resource. The rules typically state the numbers of animals allowed, where and when they may graze, which areas must be rested, and what happens to an animal found on a closed area, and the sanction is usually immediate and public rather than a fine paid to a distant authority. Monitoring works because the users see one another daily, so the cost of observing a breach is very low. The arrangement succeeds where the group is stable, the rules are clear, and the gains from compliance are shared among those who comply.

questions.explanation: Local rules, immediate peer enforcement and low monitoring costs are what make a community commons work. The item tests the institutional conditions behind successful collective management.
questions.hint: Think about who enforces the rules.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the ratio of footprint to biocapacity
questions.stem: Ratio sheet 4457 records a region with a footprint of 15.0 million global hectares and a biocapacity of 12.0 million; what is the ratio of footprint to biocapacity?
questions.explanation: Divide the footprint by the biocapacity: 15.0 divided by 12.0 gives 1.25. A ratio above one means demand exceeds what the region can regenerate in a year.
questions.hint: Divide footprint by biocapacity.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a groundwater licence protects an aquifer
questions.stem: Groundwater note 4458 asks for an explanation of how a groundwater abstraction licence protects a shared aquifer.

answer.exemplar: A groundwater licence limits the volume that may be pumped from a licensed well in a given period, which protects the aquifer in two ways. It prevents a single user from capturing the whole resource and drawing the water table below the level at which springs, wetlands and neighbouring wells depend on it. It also spreads the available water between the licensed users in a way that can be planned, so that the total pumping matches the recharge that the aquifer receives rather than exceeding it. The licence only works if the abstraction is actually metered, because an allowance that is never measured becomes a target rather than a limit, and if the permitted volumes together exceed the sustainable yield then the scheme protects nothing at all.

questions.explanation: A licence caps individual pumping so the water table is protected and total abstraction can match recharge. The item tests both the purpose and the metering condition that makes it work.
questions.hint: Think about metering and the total permitted volume.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why one treatment works cannot fix coastal eutrophication
questions.stem: Bay note 4459 asks why a single large sewage treatment works cannot remove the nutrients that cause algal blooms in a coastal bay.

options.text: Because treatment works can only remove solids and not dissolved nutrients
options.misconception: oversimplifies the capability of treatment works

options.text: Because algal blooms are caused by bacteria rather than by nutrients
options.misconception: misidentifies the cause of blooms

options.text: Because the bay receives diffuse nutrient inputs from many sources at once
Because treatment works are only built on rivers and not on coastal waters
options.misconception: invents a siting rule that does not exist

questions.explanation: A treatment works handles the sewage it receives, and the nutrients that drive blooms arrive from many diffuse sources across the catchment, so no single plant can intercept them. Treating more sewage helps little.
questions.hint: Think about the whole catchment, not one plant.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the order of treatment stages matters

stimulus.body: A cartographer's note describes a treatment works drawn in plan with the stages numbered in the order in which the flow passes through them: a screen, a grit chamber, an aeration basin, a clarifier, a sand filter and a disinfection contact tank. The note records the engineer's comment that numbering the stages out of order would save nothing, since each one exists to protect the next.

questions.stem: Order note 4460 asks which description best captures why the order of treatment stages matters.

options.text: Each stage protects the one after it by removing the material that would damage it
The order is arbitrary, because each stage removes a different pollutant and none interferes
options.misconception: ignores the interactions between stages

options.text: The most expensive stage is always placed first to spread the capital cost
options.misconception: attributes sequencing to cost timing

options.text: The final stage is always disinfection, so the sequence can be reversed from the end
options.misconception: reverses the logic of the train

questions.explanation: Sequencing exists because each stage removes something that would hinder the next: screening protects the pumps, grit removal protects the aeration, and disinfection comes last so it is not consumed. The order is functional.
questions.hint: Think about what each stage protects.
